paragraphs.heading: Numbers seen through algebra
paragraphs.text: Algebraic number theory studies whole numbers, fractions and the wider number systems built from them using the tools of abstract algebra. Questions about numbers get restated as questions about algebraic objects, such as finite fields, function fields, and number fields together with their rings of integers. Properties of those objects, such as how ideals behave or whether numbers factor in only one way, can then settle major questions, like whether a Diophantine equation has solutions.

paragraphs.heading: Old questions
paragraphs.text: Some of these questions are very old. The equation x² + y² = z² is answered by the Pythagorean triples, which the Babylonians first solved around 1800 BC. Linear equations such as 26x + 65y = 13 can be solved with the Euclidean algorithm, which dates to about the 5th century BC. Diophantus wrote the Arithmetica, though only part of it survives.

paragraphs.heading: A note in a margin
paragraphs.text: In 1637 Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of a copy of the Arithmetica a claim now called Fermat's Last Theorem. He said he had a proof that was too big for the margin. Nobody published a working proof for the next 358 years, until 1995. The search for one drove the growth of algebraic number theory in the 19th century.

paragraphs.heading: Gauss builds a system
paragraphs.text: One of the founding books of the subject is the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, which Carl Friedrich Gauss wrote in Latin at 21 and published in 1801. Before it, number theory was a scatter of separate theorems and guesses. Gauss gathered the results of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, Legendre and others, added his own, fixed weak proofs and filled gaps. His book became the starting point for later mathematicians such as Kummer, Dirichlet and Dedekind.

paragraphs.heading: Ideals and the 19th century
paragraphs.text: Ernst Kummer, in an 1843 attempt on Fermat's Last Theorem, devised ideal numbers. Richard Dedekind introduced ideals, which generalize Kummer's idea and became basic to ring theory; Hilbert and especially Emmy Noether developed them further. In 1897 David Hilbert pulled the whole field together in a report called the Zahlbericht.

paragraphs.heading: How Fermat was finally proved
paragraphs.text: Around 1955 Goro Shimura and Yutaka Taniyama noticed a possible link between two areas that looked unrelated, elliptic curves and modular forms. The idea that every elliptic curve matches a modular form became the modularity theorem. Between 1993 and 1994 Andrew Wiles proved it for semistable elliptic curves, and together with Ribet's theorem this proved Fermat's Last Theorem. His first version, announced in June 1993, had a serious gap; the fixed proof, done partly with Richard Taylor, came out in 1994 and was formally published in 1995.
